speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JUDGES ACT-FEDERAL COURT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-166, An Act to amend the Judges Act and the Federal Court Act, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to thank the Leaders and Members of both Opposition Parties for their cooperation in allowing this Bill and its companion Bill to come before us and to receive speedy passage. We are accommodating a good number of Provinces in putting this legislation through.
Bill C-166, Mr. Speaker, is an Act to amend the Judges Act and the Federal Court Act. Since it naturally falls into two segments, I will deal with each of those in turn. First, with respect to the Federal Court Act, I would point out that the Bill provides for an increase of four judges at the Federal Court of Appeal level, and two judges at the Trial Division level. Increases in the number of judges have been requested for some time by the Chief Justice and Associate Chief Justice of the Federal Court, I might add, Mr. Speaker, with a great deal of pressing and persistence on their part. This increase in the number of judges takes into account the present case load as well as the projected increase in the next few years and the desirability of reducing the reliance, to a very substantial extent, on deputy judges.
Deputy judges, Mr. Speaker, are in practice judges of the provincial Superior Courts who have retired on account of age. The Bill will correct an anomaly by extending to a judge of the federal Court of Canada the right to elect to be a supernumerary judge on the same basis as, for example, judges of the Superior Courts of the Provinces.

Mr. Speaker, the proposed amendments to the judges Bill are mainly of an administrative and technical nature. As Hon.

June 28, 1983

Members are aware, under the Constitution, the Parliament of Canada appoints the judges of superior courts and district and county courts in the provinces and provides for their salaries. In order to meet the demand in many provinces which have recently created additional positions for judges in superior and county courts or which have informed us of their intention to do so in the near future, the Government is proposing amendments to the judges Bill, authorizing salaries for the additional judges.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, we try to make some provision in advance for the Provinces by bringing the law up to date and by including the immediately pending modifications of which we have been notified by various Provinces. For example, a major reorganization is to take place this fall in the Province of Manitoba, where a new division of the Supreme Court will be created to deal with Family Court matters and where, I also understand, the County Courts and Supreme Courts will be merged. We have received advance notice of that change on the part of the Province, and so the legislation allows for that. It also allows, through the pool arrangement, for some small increase in the number of judges throughout the country at the Superior, County and District Court levels over the next few years. For these reasons, the actual net increase in the number of judges that the Bill would give us authority to appoint immediately is very much smaller than would be immediately apparent from the Bill itself.
I have already mentioned that with the reorganization four judges would be appointed to the Federal Court of Appeal and two to the Trial Division. There would also be two Supreme Court judges appointed in British Columbia and the Chief Judge of the County Courts in Manitoba. There would be five additional Queen's Bench judges and an associate Chief Justice and also an additional County Court position. There would be four Queen's Bench positions in New Brunswick, that is, for the Family Court in that Province. In Nova Scotia, there would be an additional Appeal Court Judge, two Trial Court judges and a Chief Judge of the County Courts. In Ontario, there would be two additions to the High Court and three to the County Courts as well as an acting Chief Judge. The largest number of new judgeships would be created in the Province of Quebec which has requested us to enable the appointment of nine new judges of the Superior Court level.
I might just add in conclusion that the Bill also makes technical changes and removes language in some parts of the Judges Act that may be considered sexist. These comments summarize the essential elements of the Bill and, if my colleague opposite is ready to proceed, I can sit down at this point and allow him to have the floor.

subtopic: JUDGES ACT-FEDERAL COURT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the benefit of hearing the remarks of the Minister with respect to the split portion of the Bill. I am pleased to be able to join in the debate today dealing with changes to the Judges Act and, subsequently, to deal with a Bill which will, in effect, create a new court in Canada, referred to as a tax court.
Judges Act
As the House will have noticed, the Bill was split into two portions at the insistence of my Party. There was an agreement that was finally reached prior to the introduction of the two Bills, by unanimous consent. This was because of fundamental concern expressed by Members of my Party with respect to the precedent which has been growing in the past on the part of the Government in terms of bringing in so-called omnibus legislation which purports bring in all types of amendments to a particular piece of legislation. This particular instance concerns the expansion of provincial courts at the request of the Provinces, expansion of the Federal Court at the request of the Federal Court and the creation of a new court.
We will support both of these Bills. We are not speaking against them. However, in terms of the precedent that would be established of bringing in one piece of legislation containing all of these portions, we think it is significant to stand up on each occasion ans ask-indeed, insist-that the Government bring in separate pieces of legislation with separate topics. The reason is very simple. It involves the apples and oranges concept in terms of legislation before the House.
When we are dealing with diverse, totally unrelated matters in one piece of legislation, it might well be the case, and often is the case, that Hon. Members in the House may support one portion of the Bill and oppose other provisions. As a result, we are not able to deal intelligently or responsibly with the legislation brought forward by the Government because we are dealing with a diverse number of problems. In order to make our point with respect to parts of the Bill to which we may take exception, we must vote against all the provisions of the Bill. That is simply an unacceptable way of proceeding legislatively. That is why we have insisted on the splitting of the Bill.
I think the Government is to be commended to accept what I would term as being our constructive suggestion in terms of this legislation. It has facilitated the passage of these pieces of legislation. It has allowed us to deal with them seriatim and to deal with the prinicples involved. We do support the provisions and changes to the Judges Act.
The Minister just referred to the amendments to the Judges Act. I should say at the outset that we are a little upset about the length of time it has taken for the Minister to come up with these particular amendments. Many of the Provinces involved in the Federal Court have been experiencing substantial backlogs in connection with cases coming before them and in provision of judicial services. It is clearly undesirable. The House should note the willingness of our Party to rectify the situation as quickly as possible.
There has been representation received from representatives of the Canadian Bar Association and, indeed, from representatives of provincial bars across the country, concerning the difficulties being experienced in bringing cases before various judicial bodies in each of the Provinces. The old legal axiom, which the professor who now occupies the position of Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) will understand, is that "Justice delayed is justice denied". However, I wanted to take this
COMMONS DEBATES___________ June 28, 1983
Judges Act
opportunity to address, in very few words, the new and expanding role of judges in general.
Since we are increasing the number of judges, this is an opportunity for those of us who are concerned with justice and legal affairs to consider the role of judges in our society today. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms has, of course, greatly expanded the impact of judges on our society today. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms has, of course, greatly expanded the impact of judges on our society, particularly as they relate to the criminal justice system. Opinions vary as to how great an impact there will be. Some Crown prosecutors and some police officers feel that the exclusionary rule will appear in Canada and that, as a result, we will see a host of technical acquittals and a resultant increase in crimes which go unpunished before our courts in Canada from this time on. To date, I think it is fair to say that this has not proven to be true with respect to those cases which have come before our lower courts. Flowever, many people feel that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is full of loopholes.
A suggestion exists that Clause 1 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms will severely restrict the force and effect of the Charter and that as a result, the evidentiary rules made by the Warren Court in the United States will not have a home in Canada.
In the United States, the United States Supreme Court has developed the exclusionary rule through decisions such as Mapp and Miranda preventing the use of evidence that has been collected in derogation of a person's legal rights under the Constitution. Whether Canadian courts will develop similar rules to protect citizens' rights under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is open to question. All indications to date suggest that Canadian courts will maintain their small "c" conservative leanings, although there are a number of exceptions, and particularly one reported in the Ottawa press, where a local provincial court judge excluded evidence collected through a faulty search warrant.
The American Supreme Court has been openly interventionist in its rulings on the criminal law and on other matters. Its rulings on capital punishment, abortion, busing and the environment, to name only a few, have had profound political and sociological implications.

Indeed, the traditions of the decision-making process within the U.S. courts have been different from those of our judges. American judges have shown in recent years a willingness to take an active position on political and sociological issues. The Anglo-Canadian tradition has been for the judges to confine themselves to the issue between the litigants before them, using precedent as their guide and to avoid making sweeping decisions with political implications.
It is arguable that in enacting a Charter of Rights we have only gone part way in reforming our legal system. My point is essentially that we have developed in this country a Charter of Rights that will take years to interpret. The existence of the Charter substantially increases the power of the final court of appeal in our country, the Supreme Court of Canada, to define
and delineate the rights of individual citizens. Those judges who will make these determinations are, in effect, appointed by one person, the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister ultimately determines the competence of the nominees and makes an assessment of their political, social and philosophical beliefs. Indeed, the Supreme Court of this country has, from time to time, been accused of being centralist at one time and decentralist at others. I believe the opportunity now exists for a Prime Minister to shape the day-to-day practice of rights and freedoms in this country, even to the extent of their encroachment on provincial jurisdiction. This is something that causes me major concern.
As most Members will know, United States judges are appointed to the Supreme Court by the President. But the judiciary committee of the Senate then interviews the nominees and makes a recommendation on ratification to the full Senate who then may, by simple majority, accept or reject a nomination. Fifteen presidents have seen 26 of their nominees for the Supreme Court fail to win Senate confirmation out of 139 appointments.
I would suggest to the House and to the Minister that in light of the enactment of our new Charter of Rights, we may have cause to consider what provisions we may adopt in our own country to allow elected representatives-possibly Members of Parliament or other elected officials representing various regions of our country-the opportunity of considering the social, philosophical or other views held by those nominees before their appointment to the highest court in our land is made final. Another opportunity we may consider at this time is that it may be desirable to have the Governor in Council make the nominations, at which time an appropriate committee of the House can be given the opportunity to interview and make recommendations on the appropriateness of the nomination to the Supreme Court of Canada. Indeed, the House of Commons may even be given an opportunity to vote on nominations made to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Without casting any reflection upon the competence of the Members of our Supreme Court at the present time, who are eminent and distinguished jurists, I believe that we are enter ing into a new judicial age in our country which therefore could make it the appropriate time to consider this type of investigation. Indeed, I have informally discussed this matter with more than one Member of the existing Supreme Court who have found no fault in the suggestion I have made. Furthermore, one judge was rather supportive of what I am now saying, that there should be no difficulty with an investigation not only of the qualifications and competence of nominees to the Supreme Court of Canada when a person takes that position, knowing the powers that will be vested in the Supreme Court of Canada, but to find out where they stand and have stood on issues and their attitude toward issues arising in the House.
I admit that some practical problems will exist with this method since our system involves Party disciplines and the lack of separation between the executive and legislative branches of
June 28, 1983

Government. However, a process such as the one suggested would allow an appropriate committee of the House at least to interview the nominee and discuss that nominee's qualifications and political, social and philosophical views.
Other alternatives are certainly available and have been suggested by responsible people in our country from time to time. For example, the Task Force on National Unity recommended nomination by Governor in Council following consultation with the respective Attorneys General of the Provinces. Nomination would then be ratified by the appropriate committee of the proposed council of the federation, a body which represented the Provinces at the federal level. Perhaps the Senate Reform Committee will have further recommendations with respect to the role of a reformed Senate in terms of judicial appointments in our country with regard to the enactment of the Charter of Rights.
Whatever the method, I think the important point is that it is necessary to develop a system of judicial appointments to the Supreme Court that in effect allows people who are elected the opportunity of having some input into these nominations. Again, without casting any reflection on any particular incumbent in the position of Prime Minister, I believe it is important for these decisions to be made by more than simply one person, even if that one person is the Prime Minister of our country. In developing a Charter of Rights we have only come part of the way to enhancing the rights and freedoms of Canadians. We must work as hard as we can to ensure that these rights and freedoms will be dealt with by the courts in a fair and independent fashion. Furthermore, we must ensure that they appear to be dealt with in such a fashion.
Finally, in dealing with this Bill which increases the complement of judges in various courts across our country, as the Minister pointed out, 1 want to express my concern over a matter which has received some attention recently in the public press. It concerns the whole question of the independence of the judiciary and the ability of members of the court to speak out on current political issues. I fully understand some of the frustrations felt by members of our judiciary over the traditional way in which they must deal with important political issues facing our country. Traditionally, judges simply do not speak out publicly on political issues. There is a legitimate and valid reason for this which has developed through tradition. It is that justice should not only appear to be impartial but should actually be impartial. Any suggestion that the judges have a preconceived view of the various political issues in our country cannot in any way be allowed to continue to the jeopardy of a citizen who has litigation before a court.
While there may be great sympathy for a position enunciated by members of the judiciary in this country from time to time outside the sphere of their consideration of cases before them, and while their positions may be indeed meritorious and dictate the support of people across Canada, I make the simple observation and proposition to the House that judges, by so acting, put themselves in a position where a litigant may feel he is not receiving a truly impartial hearing while pleading his case before the court if it relates to a matter on which a judge has spoken.
Judges Act
I agree with Chief Justice Laskin of the Supreme Court that the decision has to be made by those who occupy a position of judge of any of our superior courts in Canada that the only way they may address any issue is by dealing with the matter through the courts. Any other conclusion, I think, would be very seriously detrimental to our judicial system. I say to people who consider appointments to the courts that in accepting the appointment they receive some very substantial protection for their independence. They are not able to be removed arbitrarily or by any government. The only way to remove a judge of a superior court in this country is by an address by both Houses of Parliament, a resolution passed by both Houses, a very substantial protection for the judge in dealing independently with the issues before him or her without any concern for political pressure which may be imposed upon them. But by the same token, because they have that unique and unusual protection, they also have the responsibility, indeed the constraint upon them not to involve themselves in political issues from day to day.
I sometimes find it quite difficult to understand the rationale of those who speak out on the floor of the House of Commons in support of a particular judge having the ability to become involved in active debate on political issues, no matter how meritorious. I ask the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), at one time the justice critic for the New Democratic Party who represented as he did at one time Mr. Justice Berger, the rhetorical question whether in supporting Mr. Justice Berger in his right to speak out, he would feel compelled to support another judge who may speak out condemning the policies of the New Democratic Party and feel very legitimately and seriously that he was doing a public service in making a pronouncement on the policies of the New Democratic Party. I think the Hon. Member for Burnaby, or indeed the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper), or indeed the distinguished Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), or indeed the current justice critic, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), would be the first ones to stand up and say that a judge has no right to criticize the policies of the New Democratic Party, that he is wrong. I am sure they would say that there is no place for a judge in this country to involve himself in that kind of debate. When I hear from colleagues in the House of Commons to my left taking that position, it causes me a great deal of concern. It makes me wonder whether they fully understand the principles upon which judicial independence in our system is based.
I have spoken a little longer than I intended, Mr. Speaker. But this is one of the few opportunities that one has to talk about judges. I do not want to cast any reflection on the Minister or the Government by saying that we in the Opposition are not often consulted about judicial appointments. We hear about them. Press releases come across our desks. From time to time I know that judges appointed by this Government have had some past affiliation with the governing Party. It is

June 28, 1983
Judges Act
not an unheard of proposition that that is the case, I simply say to the Minister that I hope after the next election when we are in government we will take a far broader view with respect to the responsibilities and try to be as apolitical as we can. Mind you, as has been pointed out by our new Leader there are many highly qualified people who at one time or another supported the Conservative Party who are still available for judicial appointments, and I would not want to deny them that responsibility. Therefore, I do not want to tie myself down too closely by saying that we would not appoint any Conservatives because that would be wrong-headed and unfortunate. I simply say to the Minister that while we petition him to develop the process, there has been some progress with respect to the whole process of judicial selection of judges in Canada. An attempt has been made for greater consultation with various provincial bars and the Canadian Bar Association, and I think this is an admirable development concerning judicial appointments in our country.
With the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and for a variety of reasons, the role of the judiciary in our country is expanding in importance. Judges are becoming involved, as they are in many issues, in the interpretations they bring down which affect the daily lives of Canadians, and it is important that we deal with these matters in terms of getting the best people possible appointed to the bench. We should be tireless in our efforts and supportive of each other as much as possible on a non-partisan basis to get the best people possible to serve as judges in the courts of our land.
With those few remarks I conclude my observations with respect to this Bill, but again I wish to assure the Minister of the position we have taken. We are prepared to let this Bill go through all stages today in order to relieve somewhat the pressure on the courts across the country with respect to the workload they experience.

Mr. Speaker, most of the matters which are dealt with in the legislation before us are technical. They are not controversial, they are not partisan. I presume the Minister of Justice (Mr. Mac-Guigan), in consultation with his provincial counterparts, decided that a certain number of judges is needed in each Province and there is good reason for this. Likewise, for the reorganization into the tax court there is good reason for it and it is something we can all support.
I want to make a couple of comments about judicial appointments, although my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper), will be making a few more.
I do recall, apropos of a few remarks of the previous speaker, that in making representations to the last Conservative Prime Minister about judicial appointments, I pointed out that those appointments would all be going to the Conservative Party after years of going all to the Liberal Party and I suggested that appointments might be based relative to population. I suggested that we might concede that a certain number of eligible people would have no political affiliation and that the other appointments should be distributed roughly according to representation in popular vote. 1 did not get anywhere with this
proposal. The former Prime Minister did not think that such a reasonable proposal was worth considering.
The Minister of Justice has made reference to improving some of the sexist language in the Judges Act. I want to commend him for that. However, I want to point out that it is a very minor change he has made so far and it is far from the most important one. The language is still framed in the masculine. The judges are all "he". Of course, this is largely true. Most judges are men, but clearly this is one of the points we want to address. Women should be well represented in the judiciary and so far they are not.
The one change the Minister did make concerns pensions. The phrase now, instead of being "widow's pension", is "pension for the surviving spouse". It is an important principle that widowers be treated on the same basis as widows. Let us not be foolish about this and think that this will address any dire social need. I doubt whether there is any widower of a woman judge who is in desperate need of the pension, and 1 doubt any injustice would have continued by keeping the old language. What we need is a much more comprehensive change to nonsexist language throughout. I would refer the Minister to the guidelines established by the status of women in Canada which were released very recently. These were prepared for what was called federal Government communications. They were not directed toward legislation. But the same principle holds. They are very good guidelines. I would suggest they be consulted and in the future the Ministry of Justice phrase its legislation in non-sexist terms. This is not just a matter of symbols, Mr. Speaker. Symbols themselves are important. But judges make decisions regarding people's lives. We have had disastrous decisions in the past regarding women. There has been a long series of women's equality cases. They have gone through the courts all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court of Canada has a disastrous record in dealing with women's equality right back to the old Persons case. Women were not persons within the lifetime of many Members of this House. In the Judges Act, women are still not persons. They are nobodies. I think we have to assume this affects judges' thinking.
I plan to bring in some amendments at Committee of the Whole stage, but 1 would like to comment briefly on the rationale behind them. There are two amendments concerning pensions. First, there is a section which eliminates the widow's pension, or what will be called the surviving spouse's pension when the legislation is passed, if the widow or surviving spouse remarries. Clearly there is the idea of a widow being a dependent, and the pension is only for the time that the widow is a dependent. This is a very false idea.
We have a notion that marriage is a partnership of equals. In the case where the judge has a homemaker spouse who did not go into the paid labour force, that person is dependent on the judge and the judge's pension, but that person has also made a contribution. For example, that person has probably raised children over a number of years and done a great deal of
June 28, 1983

work for the couple. That is normally recognized by having a pension as a result, but we do not see this; the person does not get a pension in her own name if her husband dies and she remarries. She loses the pension, which is extremely unfair to her. It may mean that some women in these circumstances who would like to remarry will not remarry because they cannot afford to lose that pension for which they have worked and to which they have contributed for many, many years by their work in the marriage.
The other pension amendment concerns the pension of the judge being split between the two spouses when the spouse reaches the age of 65. This is a proposal which is being considered for many pension plans including the Canada Pension Plan. It is in the green paper and has been discussed wherever pensions were under discussion. This amendment recognizes that a couple is a partnership of equals. They each work, they each contribute, and they should each benefit. Clearly it would not be fair if the spouse did not split her or his pension in the circumstances, but it would be eminently fair in the case of the homemaker spouse for whom there is no pension at all, or a spouse who is in the paid labour force and splits her or his pension at the same time.
I think they are very reasonable and very important amendments. Judges should have a model pension scheme. They make decisions about pensions which affect all other Canadian men and women. They have made bad decisions in the past. Why did we have the cases of Murdoch, Leatherdale and Rathwell? Why did we have these cases where the contribution of women was not understood and was underestimated? Judges' own pensions underestimate the contribution of women. We only have to look at their own scheme, which Parliament provided, to see that women are not equal beings. It is very important in the area of pensions that the provisions for judges be the best possible ones in our society, that they really be just and fair.
I will be introducing these amendments when the Bill is being considered in Committee of the Whole. I do not want to continue any further now. We will be supporting the Bill. As I said, most of its provisions are non-controversial. I hope to obtain the support of the Conservative Party and, indeed, of the Government on the two amendments that I will introduce.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues in the Conservative Party and in the Liberal Party for allowing me the courtesy of making a few short remarks in this debate without in any way whatsoever delaying the movement of the legislation.
What I want to comment upon concerns the process of appointing judges in the country. As I understand it, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appoints judges and there is no public process through which the suitability of judges for the bench is examined before he makes appointments. While this may have been appropriate throughout our judicial practice in the past, I would suggest that, with the introduction of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Constitution which will now
Judges Act
contain provisions with regard to aboriginal rights, it is important that there be an opportunity for a full and open exploration of the views and attitudes of judges before they are appointed, simply because of the fact that indeed they are independent, as they should be, after their appointment.
I must say as well that the provisions in the Constitution with regard to sexual equality demand a full exploration of the views of possible appointees to the bench before they are appointed.
It is crucial that all Canadians understand that when they go before the courts they will be treated fairly and will be seen to be treated fairly. I want to give an example by referring to a recent event that pointed to the need to examine the whole question of how we appoint judges in Canada. I am thinking of the comments in the last few months of Mr. Justice Monnin in the Province of Manitoba. He was reported in the newspapers as having said something to the effect that if he had to throw out of court all the evidence of drunken Indians there would be nothing left. Of course the native community reacted to these comments with anger and dismay, quite rightly so.
I do not want to comment with regard to the quoted statements of Justice Monnin, but I want to say that they point to the need for a full and open process of appointing judges so that all citizens can have full confidence in the judiciary. After these comments were reported, a complaint was made to the judicial council; of course no action was taken. After that the Prime Minister, with no public input, appointed the same Justice as Chief Justice for the Province of Manitoba, to the surprise and dismay of many residents of that Province.
It is time for an open and public process for the appointment of judges. It is important that all citizens feel and know that they will be treated fairly when they enter the courts of the land. This is particularly important now that we have the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and there will be provisions in the Constitution with regard to aboriginal rights.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AN ACT RESPECTING THE TAX COURT OF CANADA AND TO AMEND THE FEDERAL COURT ACT, THE JUDGES ACT AND THE UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AND TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-167, An Act respecting the Tax Court of Canada and to amend the Federal Court Act, the Judges Act and the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very conscious of the importance of not detaining the House very long. However, I think I should outline very briefly the salient points of Bill C-167 and the reasons for the changes introduced by that Bill.
First, the Tax Review Board is continued under the name of the Tax Court of Canada as a court of record. We believe that such a change in the name of this tribunal will improve the perception by the general public of its nature. The Tax Review Board has been considered by many taxpayers as an arm of the Department of National Revenue or of the Government of Canada. The present name of the Tax Review Board is known to have given the mistaken impression that the Board had an interest in the outcome of actions before it.
Tax Court of Canada
This change will also reflect the exclusively judicial nature of this tribunal. It is inappropriate to maintain an impression that it is an agency or a board of the federal Government rather than a court of law.
The conversion of this Board into a court of law had been recommended by the Canadian Bar Association to the Royal Commission on Taxation (the Carter Commission). In turn, the latter commission, among its many recommendations which gave rise to the 1972 tax reform, proposed the creation of a tax court. More recently, the Canadian Bar Association was consulted by my predecessor and that association fully endorsed the proposal regarding the change in name and status of the Board.
I stress, however, that the Government does not want to make more difficult the taxpayers' access to this tribunal, nor does it want to introduce formality in the conduct of the board's proceedings-quite the contrary. It is provided in subclause 14(1) of the Bill that an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada does not require any special form of pleadings. Subclause 14(2) sets out that the Court is not bound by the technical rules of evidence. The same Subclause goes even further and states that all appeals are to be dealt with by the courts as informally and expeditiously as circumstances and considerations of fairness permit.
From Clause 15, it is apparent that the taxpayer may appeal to the Court in person or may be represented by a lawyer, friend or any other person of his choice. The Court cannot award costs on the disposition of an appeal. The substance of all these provisions is now found in the Tax Review Board Act.
A second change proposed by the Bill has to do with certain amendments to Part IV of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971. It should be recalled that Part IV of the latter statute is, at the present time, administered by the Department of National Revenue. Appeals under that part are now heard by umpires who, in practice, are the judges of the Trial Division of the Federal Court of Canada.
The transfer of jurisdiction to the Tax Court of Canada is desirable on account of the fact that the handling of UI appeals on the coverage side more properly fits a court like this tribunal than a court of superior jurisdiction like the Federal Court of Canada.
The appeal system against a decision of the tribunal of first instance in appeals under Part IV of the Act will be simplified in that all decisions of the Tax Court of Canada will be the subject matter of a single review under Section 28 of the Federal Court Act. At the present time, the decision of an umpire with regard to an appeal under Part IV of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, can be appealed pursuant to Section 86 of the latter Act to the Pensions Appeal Board with leave of that Board in respect of a question of law involving

June 28, 1983
Tax Court of Canada
Section 3 of that Act and can be subject as well to an application for review under Section 28 of the Federal Court Act on all other questions involved in that decision. It is to be noted that there is no change in the appeal system regarding benefit cases.
Part III of the Judges Act is also amended so as to entrust the Commissioner for Federal Judicial Affairs with the management of the affairs of this tribunal. The considerations which prompted the Government a few years ago to transfer the administrative duties and functions relative to the staff of the Federal Court of Canada from the Department of Justice to the Commissioner for Federal Judicial Affairs are equally valid in this case. This is done with a view to further enhancing the independence of the judiciary in Canada and ensuring to the greatest possible extent, consistent with the principles of the ministerial responsibility of a parliamentary system of Government, that the administration of judicial affairs is to be separate and apart from the administration of the affairs of the executive branch of the Government.

Finally, the Government is proposing to increase the number of members of this tribunal from seven to twelve. The rapid increase in appeals from income tax payments and the new jurisdiction of this court with respect to appeals under Part IV of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, are ample justification for this increase. In this respect, I would like to note that the number of members has remained the same since the Act was passed in December 1970.

Mr. Speaker, I commend this Bill to the support of the House, and again I express my gratitude to the Members of the Opposition for their co-operation and for being prepared to consider this Bill at all stages today.

subtopic: AN ACT RESPECTING THE TAX COURT OF CANADA AND TO AMEND THE FEDERAL COURT ACT, THE JUDGES ACT AND THE UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AND TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate being afforded the opportunity to show the spirit of co-operation for which I and my Party are known, by zooming through this legislation with dispatch. Nonetheless, we do take these pieces of legislation very seriously. I know that the kind of co-operation I have demonstrated today will be reflected by the Government House Leader tomorrow when I introduce a Private Members' Bill which will ask for unanimous consent of the House. I simply enter into my remarks on that basis so that he will understand the import of my imprecations.
1 would like to talk about the creation of a Tax Court in Canada as contemplated by this Bill. It was stated by the Minister in a press release of May 25, 1983, that the Tax Review Board is to be designated as a court of law and the board members are to be made judges so as to dispel "the impression that it is merely an agency of the federal Government with an interest in the outcome of the actions that are brought before it."
On the basis of my experience, Mr. Speaker, I must agree, and I am sure Members of the House of Commons will understand, with the move which is now being made because of the growing number of appeals of income tax and other tax related cases. The litigants involved in these cases want to have
at least the impression that there will be an impartial adjudication of their problems.
The quasi-judicial or administrative board approach of the Tax Review Board, while again being served by distinguished Canadians, has lent itself to the unfortunate perception that the Board has been an extension of the Department of National Revenue. Indeed, there is some basis upon which the litigant might have some apprehensions in this regard, because dealing with a quasi-judicial or administrative tribunal is not the same as dealing with a court of record.
In a court of record, the judge has very substantial independence in terms of tenure and there is very little possibility of Government influence under normal circumstances. I say in the spirit of co-operation that it should not be possible to influence judges of a court of record even by a telephone call from a member of the Treasury Branch or a Minister of the Crown. The idea is that a judicial member of a court of record does have independence in terms of that kind of political pressure which, from time to time, might in some circumstances be attempted to be exercised on that person.
In the case of an administrative tribunal, there are considerations of reappointment and of benefits. Indeed there has been some litigation with respect to the independence of the courts in Canada in recent months that has challenged whether or not provincially appointed judges are truly independent because of the fact that matters of benefits and income, of determination of their circuits and workload, are in fact regulated by a Civil Servant or a member of the Department of Justice in a particular Province.
We are then asked to create a new court to dispel the impression that the Tax Review Board was not a truly independent tribunal. How does this Bill seek to achieve that objective? First, all current members of the Tax Review Board will continue in office as judges of the Tax Court. The current chairman will be renamed as Chief Judge of the Court and the assistant chairman who is, incidentally, a former associate Deputy Attorney General and was appointed on June 6 of this year, will be renamed and appointed as Associate Chief Judge of the Court.
Second, the Bill establishes the qualifications for appointment to the Court. One must be or have been a judge of a Superior, County or District Court in Canada or be a barrister or advocate of at least ten years' standing in the Bar of any of the Provinces. Yet in Section 24 of the Bill it is stated that all Tax Review Board members would continue in office despite any of the Bill's provisions such as the varied qualifications required of a Tax Court Judge.
While I understand the fact that there must be a transition period, initially the same crowd will continue on under new appointments. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, Tax Review Board members are exempted from the residency requirements of the Bill. Judges must reside within the National Capital Region or within 40 kilometres of it. This exemption did not appear in the omnibus Bill C-159, but it has been slipped into the new split Bill.
June 28, 1983

What of the procedures that will be followed by the new court? Will they change the impression that judges are merely extensions of the Government or departments of the Government? At the present time the Board is not bound by any legal or technical rules of evidence in its hearings. Further, its empowering statute states that it must dispose of all appeals informally and expeditiously, keeping in mind considerations of fairness and the circumstances of the case.
The new tax court will hold hearings on appeals under the same set of rules as those which govern the Board. Indeed, Clause 14(2) of the Bill is identical in every respect with Section 9(2) of the Tax Review Board Act. We are, therefore, creating a court of law which will not be bound by legal and technical rules of evidence.
It is interesting to note as well that Clause 18 of the Bill precludes the tax court from awarding costs on the disposition of an appeal.
The point is, Mr. Speaker, that the Government cannot have it both ways. I want to make this observation for the consideration of the Minister. On the one hand the Minister claims to be dispelling an impression that the Tax Review Board is an agency of the Government. He is attempting to do this through the creation of a tax court. On the other hand, we find that all Board members will continue as judges, that they need not meet the qualifications of judges and that they need not meet the residency requirements of judges.
Further, the rights of litigants before the court in terms of the rules of evidence and the awarding of costs in appropriate circumstances, are cast aside. Clearly the Minister is merely changing the name of the Tax Review Board, cloaking it with the distinguished character of a court while in many respects leaving it substantially unchanged. This reflects not only on the legitimacy of the tax court but, it seems to me, the Government is relying more on form than on substance with respect to this Bill. I have serious concern about the legitimacy of the tax court but I am also concerned that a move like this might affect the operation of that court.
In our system if a court is to be a court of record with judges appointed, there is protection in terms of the independence of the judges and, therefore, a very dramatic and substantial effort has to be undertaken if a member of any court in this country has to be removed from the bench. By the same token, when there is that kind of protection the judges of the court are normally obliged to abide by certain rules of evidence and procedure. This protection is not provided for lawyers or any elite group; it is there so there are clearly defined rules to ensure that a litigant's case will receive proper and impartial consideration. That is the purpose of rules of evidence. They are not there to accommodate lawyers or judges so that they can develop their own jargon.
There is a good reason for rules of evidence, Mr. Speaker, and I want to draw my observation to the attention of the Minister. I understand the necessity for informality at the Tax Review Board so that people who appear without counsel are
Tax Court of Canada
not intimidated. But I wonder whether, going the court route, we should not give serious consideration to monitoring the operation of that court. Perhaps we should reconsider the question of whether that informality is appropriate for a court of record.
I make that observation without drawing any conclusion. When I read the Bill it occurred to me that if we are going the court route we should go the whole way. There may be some places where we will need rules of evidence. I know the Canada Evidence Act is before the Senate at the present time and debate is going on there with respect to rules of evidence and the way judicial proceedings should be conducted. I think that is the appropriate place to have a full and proper consideration of the way the court would be conducted rather than changing the Tax Review Board to a tax court and leaving it with its own informal procedures and technical rules of operation.
If a situation should occur where a judge of that court, due to lack of confidence or some other reason, were to abuse his or her position, the old remedies are not available to the Department of Justice or the Department of National Revenue, or whoever administers the Tax Review Board, to deal with that problem. These will be independent judges, free from interference by the Department of Justice or the Department of National Revenue. I am somewhat concerned about going part way on the rules of evidence and technical requirements of the new tax court.
I know the Minister is giving serious consideration to judicial appointments and my remarks apply to the previous Bill which dealt with the expansion of Superior Courts and the Federal Court as well as to this Bill. The Minister will be supported in any move to increase the number of women appointed to the bench. I think that is a nonpartisan issue in the House. All Parties are in favour of increasing the number of women in the courts of the country. I have lectured at the College of Law at the University of Saskatchewan and have been amazed to see the transformation that has taken place. The number of women enrolled in colleges of law in this country has grown to the point where there are as many women as men. Generally speaking, they do exceptionally well; only a few do approximately as well as I did when I went through law school. Most women are very determined, dedicated and outstanding students.
In my own City and indeed, in my own firm, I have been amazed at the transformation that has taken place in the way that women have become leading counsel and solicitors. When my sister graduated in law in the late 1960s there was still resistance to women lawyers in law offices. If a client was asked to see a woman lawyer in the firm it was almost like asking them if they would like a case of the flu. You could see them shrug and move away. That kind of stereo-typing has gone. Women are actively, effectively and aggressively participating as members of the Bar. But only 4 per cent of our judges are women, Mr. Speaker.
I want to point out to the Minister that this Party would be very supportive of the appointment of more women to the

June 28, 1983
Tax Court of Canada
bench. The Minister will find that there now is a larger body of women to choose from because the increase in the number of women graduates from law school means there are many with ten or 15 years experience at the Bar who can meet the 10-year requirement for appointment to the Superior Court.
I wanted to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, some of my concerns about some aspects of the Bill. We are prepared to support the Bill and see it passed, however, I would hope that the Minister, on behalf of the Government, would state that it will be monitoring the operation of this new tax court for the purpose of determining whether or not the informality and the appropriateness of that kind of informality for which the Tax Revenue Board is known will be considered, in light of the new status of the Court as a court of record.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subtopic: CANADA-GERMANY TAX AGREEMENT ACT, 1982 MEASURE TO AVOID DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
that Bill S-24, an Act to implement an agreement between Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to taxes on income and certain other taxes, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am mindful of the wish of the House to have the time of remarks kept to a minimum. I do have a few brief remarks and I understand there are one or two Hon. Members as well who would like to make comment.
June 28, 1983

The purpose of Bill S-24, Mr. Speaker, is to implement an agreement between Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to taxes on income and certain other taxes. In addition, the Bill provides that the Governor in Council may, subject to resolution of Parliament, give effect by Order in Council to any supplementary agreement.
On this latter point, Mr. Speaker, Bill S-24, as passed by the Senate, is different from that before us, and introduced by the Government, and I will have a few comments to make on that point.
When in force, the proposed agreement will replace the 1956 agreement between the two countries. The agreement with Germany follows the pattern of similar agreements concluded by Canada over the past several years. I believe there are 32 such agreements with other countries.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) for assisting the Minister in preparation of the form of this Bill here before us. There are a number of changes which had to be reviewed. The Senate material had to be reviewed and the work which he gave in preparation to getting to this point has to be commended. In addition, I would at the same time like to commend the efforts of the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) who, as Hon. Members know, has taken an interest in this subject and has been of assistance to the Government in seeing that the legislation has reached this point for conclusion.
This agreement, Mr. Speaker, generally provides that dividends can be taxed in the country of source at a maximum rate of 15 per cent. A general rate of 15 per cent is also provided in the case of interest arising from one country and paid to a resident of another country. However, there is an exemption for certain types of interest such as that paid on Government bonds or to the Export Development Corporation, or the German equivalent of same. Patent royalties and technical know-how payments are subject to a maximum tax of 10 per cent in the source country, and copyright royalties in respect of literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works are exempt. Capital gains from disposition of real property or business assets and of shares in companies, the assets of which consist principally of real estate, may be taxed in the country in which the property is situate. Pensions and annuities arising in one country and paid to a resident of the other country may generally be taxed in the country in which they arise. However, war veterans' pensions and benefits under the social securities legislation in the country will be taxable only in that country. I can understand, Mr. Speaker, therefore, the interest and the consent of Hon. Members in seeing this legislation passed. It should be noted that this provision will be applicable from 1978, and it will be of benefit to several thousand residents of German origin. The agreement also contains the usual provisions concerning relief from double taxation, non-discrimination, mutual agreement procedure and exchange of information.
Canada-Germany Tax Agreement Act, 1982
I want to go back now, Mr. Speaker, to the question of supplementary agreements. The Bill introduced in the Senate on February 2, 1982, contained clauses designed to ensure that the agreement can be kept up to date as a result of changes in the tax systems of Canada or Germany. These clauses ere in line with those approved by Parliament in the past with some 32 countries. But during the Senate proceedings, the Senators made a number of amendments to the Bill. They were primarily concerned with the power of the Government to amend the agreement by means of a supplementary agreement made by order of the Governor in Council. In order to limit the power given to the executive by the Bill to modify or amend the Canada-Germany Taxation Agreement, they made the following change by amending Clause 5(1) to provide that a supplementary agreement:
-shall not, in any manner, impose a greater tax burden on any person than the one to which such person might be subject, but for this Act, as may be amended from time to time-
The second change was to amend the provisions of Clause 6 relating to the negative resolution procedure that applied to the supplementary agreement inter alia through reducing the number of Members in both the House and the Senate who could initiate the procedure I just referred to.
The first mentioned amendment, Mr. Speaker, is not acceptable in that it carries the clear implication that a double taxation treaty can impose taxes, whereas it is generally recognized and accepted by the courts that such a treaty can only reduce or relieve taxes. While I would be quite prepared to accept the addition of some language to Clause 5(1) that would meet the legitimate concern of the Senators, by qualifying the power of the executive to revoke existing agreements, the specific language passed by the Senate is not acceptable to the Government and must be removed.
With respect to the amendment moved in the Senate concerning the negative resolution, I see some merit in keeping them as they represent an improvement over the one previously agreed to by Parliament. The only difficulty I have is with the reduction from 50 and 20 to 20 and 10 in the number of Members or Senators respectively required to file a motion. The Government has proposed a compromise, which I understand is acceptable to Members of the House. So I am suggesting a compromise solution of 30 and 15 respectively.
Germany has been ready for some time to ratify the agreement and is anxious to put it into force, as are we. The amendments introduced by the Senate have to be considered by law officers of the Crown. Department officials and I have reviewed them, assisted by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher), and we believe that it is now time to have this Bill passed and the agreement put into force.
I will conclude by thanking the Hon. Members for their support of this legislation as it will help a considerable number of Canadians. At the appropriate stage in Committee of the Whole I will move two amendments which Members have seen.

June 28, 1983
Canada-Germany Tax Agreement Act, 1982

subtopic: CANADA-GERMANY TAX AGREEMENT ACT, 1982 MEASURE TO AVOID DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will join in this great spirit of co-operation in which the House finds itself this evening and make my brief comments with respect to this important measure and landmark agreement between Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany.
The Minister has given a fair assessment of what the Bill is intended to do. He has also given a fair assessment of the difficulty associated with bringing this Bill before the House for ratification, and a fair assessment of the amendments he thought, and indeed, I agree, were necessary to improve the Bill so that it can receive the ratification of the House. Indeed, the Minister has given a fair assessment of my involvement with the Bill and I thank him very much for making reference to that.
It was on July 17, 1981, Mr. Speaker, during the Summit Conference held here in Ottawa that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of Canada and the Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Germany signed this agreement which, in the opinion of many, was long overdue. Canada already has, as the Minister says, about 32 agreements like this. Indeed, there was a previous agreement with the Federal Republic of Germany dating back to 1956. However, there was one serious flaw or shortcoming in that agreement which has been corrected in Article 18, the most important Article in this Bill, dealing with the double taxation of pensions.
There are roughly 1.5 million people in this country who are Canadian citizens of German ancestry, many of whom have earned certain pension rights in the old country and are entitled to benefits. There are also German nationals living out their declining years with their relatives here in our country.
The Bill was introduced in the Senate on February 2, 1982, which was about the same time or shortly after the Parliament of the Federal Republic of Germany ratified the agreement. On July 7, 1982, the Senate passed the Bill but, as the Minister pointed out, it had certain flaws. It took until now to correct those flaws and get the Bill before this House.
For some of the people who have written and telephoned me over the last two years it is difficult to understand why it should take so long. Indeed, some of them suspected ill intent by the Government and accused us of discrimination against German nationals because of all the agreements we have with other countries. I can assure these people today that there was no ill intent. The Bill had some real difficulties.
It is particularly difficult for German nationals to understand this because many of them left Germany to escape bureaucracy and over-regulation. They came to this country because there is greater freedom and control over one's own personal life. They have now experienced bureaucracy in Canada. It can be equally insensitive to the real needs of people as other bureaucracies.
As the Minister has outlined, the Bill affects capital, taxes on total income, total capital, or elements of income or capital, including taxes on capital gains, taxes on the total amount of wages or salaries paid by enterprises as well as taxes on capital appreciation. Because all of these things fall under the Income Tax Act in our own country, that would be the only Act which
will be effective. In the Federal Republic of Germany it will be the income tax or the Einkommensteuer provision, the corporation tax of Koerperschaftsteuer, the capital tax or the Vermoegensteuer, and finally the trade tax or Gewerbesteuer, with which German nationals are familiar.
Even though this measure is long overdue, I am delighted to be able to participate this afternoon in the passage of this Bill through all stages, and to report tomorrow to the many people who have written to me and many of my colleagues on both sides of the House that this matter has finally been dealt with and ratified.
Incidentally, in the case of the double taxation of pensions, the measure is retroactive to 1978. So, many people affected by this Bill will indeed get a sizeable refund on taxes they have paid over the years. I am sure the Minister will join me in wishing these people many happy years during which they can spend those hard-earned dollars.
Let me just close by thanking my colleagues on this side of the House, our House Leader and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) for making this special accommodation this afternoon, one day before recess, to assure that this matter will be dealt with in this tax year. I give my particular thanks to the Minister for his assistance in making this accommodation.

The legislation will avoid double taxation as it affects pensions in particular, retroactive to 1978. While the legislation is long overdue, I am sure that the people who are affected, those who have been writing to us all and calling for changes in the legislation, all citizens of German ancestry in Canada, would simply say "Danke" to this Chamber.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if any Member of the House had any doubt as to whether or not there was such a thing as eternal life, one need only look at some of the programs and statutes that have found their way into the books of Canada. Certainly during my ten and one-half years in Parliament, there have been very few instances when Parliament has actually acted to reduce the encumbrances that have been hoisted on the Canadian people by passive Parliaments or that have been added in the terms of new costly programs.
To the extent to which anything is being done this evening in repealing statutes which are obsolete and no longer used, some progress is being made. However there should be no confusion between what is before us today and any substantive meaningful attempt at regulatory reform. Indeed, to the extent to which the Government is trying to sell this Bill before us tonight as regulatory reform by proposing that this in some way meets the demands for regulatory reform from Canadian people at the present time, it is misleading Canadians and putting something before the Parliament of Canada which does not achieve the purpose which it has been discussing. When the Minister spoke to this Bill at second reading, he spoke as if the initiative had begun in the fall of 1980. In fact, the initiative for an omnibus repeal Bill began under the Clark Government. I was the Minister responsible for regulatory reform and, in conjunction with Senator Flynn, who was the Minister of Justice at the time, it was our intention to introduce an omnibus repeal Bill which would sweep away many of the statutes which had become obsolete and no longer used. Unfortunately, we were prevented from doing that by the election.
That was only to be one very minor part of regulatory reform. There were far more substantive issues to be addressed. I might add that there are far more substantive things that remain to be done today, some four years later.
During the tenure of our Government we proposed to Parliament a sunset Bill which would restore to Members of Parliament the right and responsibility of reviewing programs and statutes which had been put in place in order to determine whether they were still needed and still provided the best
vehicle to serve the needs that Canadians had expressed. Nothing has been done by the Government to put sunset legislation into place. That initiative simply died with the death of the Clark Government.
There are other initiatives that were intended as well. We had expected that a major program of regulatory reform would be undertaken in many instances to streamline and make more fair and efficient the process of regulations.
I want to express my disappointment tonight, as chairman of the Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, that notwithstanding the fact that the committee's fourth report was introduced some years ago in which we made major recommendations for improvements to the process of regulations in Canada that would be more fair to permit Parliament to discharge its responsibility to the people of Canada, virtually nothing has been done by the Government to act on that report. Indeed, when I moved concurrence in that report, the Government voted to prevent the matter from even being debated. We simply have not heard of it since that time.
We had also intended to undertake a program of deregulation to return to the market place and to individual Canadians the right to determine in so many instances what the policies would be and how they would live their lives. With the election of this Liberal Government we have found that that initiative has faltered. We have found vast new amounts of Government regulation, Government spending and vast intrusion by the Government into the day-to-day lives of Canadians.
What has the Government done. It has taken one positive step. It has proposed a regulatory calendar, which again is an idea of which we approved. It would give some notice to Canadians of proposed regulatory initiatives by the Government over the course of a year. It is a sensible move and it is hard to understand why the Government would take so long to act upon it.
It has proposed this measure which would do away with some obsolete statutes which have been long since forgotten. 1 understand that some parliamentarians would show concern about repealing an Act for the control and extrapolation of foot and mouth disease. I am relieved, from reading the notes, that the provisions of this Act have been incorporated into the Animal Disease and Protection Act and that Parliament is safe from having these provisions simply stripped away from us.
No doubt Members will be disappointed to discover that the Volunteer Bounty Act of 1908 is being swept away. According to the notes, the purpose of this Act was to grant volunteers who served with the British Forces in South Africa during the Boer War between 1899 and 1902 domicile in Canada, or with the Canadian Corps, two adjoining quarter sections of Dominion lands or $160 in script in lieu of the land.
There are other Acts which I am sure Members will be astonished to discover are being swept away. For instance, there is the Gold Clauses Act. There is the Hemp Bounties Act of 1923. It is an Act which authorized the payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of bounties for hemp grown,
June 28, 1983

manufactured and sold in Canada. Because these bounties were payable only during 1926 and 1933, the Act is considered spent. There are apparently no outstanding claims for bounties.
It will come as a shock to Members that all of these measures are being swept away, when I know that so many of us have mentioned support for these measures in our brochures at election time. We will have to tell our constituents that with this Government, so vigilant and anxious to regulate and propose programs, if any gaps are found it will quickly move into the void and provide the services which Canadians did not realize were being provided previously by these programs.
What else have the Liberals done? They have changed the jargon. We heard before about deregulation. The jargon was then changed to regulatory reform. I think that was the expression we used in our tenure in Government; it made sense. They have two new buzzwords. Regulatory reform has been dropped, and now the in-jargon is managing regulation. One can speculate on what that really means. There is a better one; re-regulation. I believe I heard the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) use that expression the other day. It may seem that the difference is only semantic or an exchange of euphemisms, but in fact the difference is more profound than that. It goes to the philosophy of the Parties in power.
We were determined to do two things during our term in office. The first was to make more fair and more effective the process of regulation and to plug Parliament back into the picture to ensure that Members of Parliament would do the job they were sent down here to do. The second thing, one which was at least as important, was to begin to roll back some of the regulatory intrusion into the day-to-day lives of Canadians and to return to the efficiency of the marketplace for making many of the decisions which are now made by the Government. That is what deregulation means. It has to do with one's philosophy, whether one feels that Government is too big, too costly and too intrusive into the day-to-day lives of Canadians. That was our feeling and it remains our feeling. It would be a priority of a Progressive Conservative Government to begin the work of deregulation.
We now hear about managing regulation or about reregulation. We have a Government in power with the philosophy that perhaps it will tinker in the periphery. It is prepared to act boldly to abolish statutes which are long since obsolete and which no Member of Parliament even remembered were on the books. It will act boldly in that area. It is prepared to talk and to commission a task force on regulatory reform- which has come and gone with very little to show for it. It is prepared to talk about processes, but it is not prepared to act. Most important, it is not prepared to take action to reduce the size of Government.
The other measure the Liberals undertook which would be of some value to Canadians was the measure to shorten the period during which individuals or corporations would have to retain records. That is helpful. Nobody quarrels with that, but
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
it was not a great blow being struck for the people of Canada to have a sensible measure like that initiated.
If we want to determine whether or not there has been any progress in the past three and a half years in the whole issue of regulatory reform I suppose the best way would be to ask ourselves to remember what Canada was like three and a half years ago. If we left the country then and returned this summer, would we find a country which is more encumbered by regulation or less encumbered? Would we find a Parliament that is more able to do its job of holding the Government to account or less able? Would we find a Government that is extended even further into the day-to-day lives of people, making decisions which people should be making for themselves, or would we find a Government that is smaller? Would we find a Government that is more costly and that has confiscated more of our national wealth, or would we find a Government in which spending has been brought under control and has begun to lead by example instead of by simply preaching the virtues of restraint?
In each of those criteria we would find that we have a Government which has grown in size, in cost and in intrusiveness, at the expense of the wealth and the liberty of the people of Canada; at the expense as well of Members of Parliament who believe that it is their responsibility to hold the Government to account, to examine Government proposals, to sweep away from time to time measures which have long since outlived their usefulness, and to protect the civil liberties of Canadians. The simple honest truth is that we have not done our job in this Parliament; we have allowed the Government to usurp unto itself more power, more of the national wealth.
What is the reason for that? Will regulatory reform, regulatory management, or whatever jargon, succeed? Will this program succeed under the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) and under this Government? I fear it will not. I fear that the next time we will see any bold initiative taken for regulatory reform, it will be with a change in Government. What we have in this Minister and what we have in this Government is an administration that believes in increasing the size of Government and in increasing its own power at the expense of ordinary Canadians.
All the incentives, all the rewards and all the momentum in Government is for Government to become more intrusive, not less intrusive; to spend more, not less; to become more bureaucratic, not less bureaucratic. As politicians, the rewards received are for proposing new programs, not for taking programs away. Bureaucrats are judged on the strength and the size of their budgets, the size of the complement working for them and the extent of their responsibilities. Ministers are judged in much the same way. All the rewards in our system are for increasing the size and cost of Government.
The only way we could hope to reverse that momentum and get Government moving in the other direction would be to have the political will, where politicians exert their control on the machinery, where they demonstrate that they believe it is time to swing the pendulum away from Government and back toward the people of Canada, and that it is time to reduce the

The Minister who is trying to drown me out from his seat has the temerity to say that the Government has a willingness to share power with Parliament and with the people of Canada. Ultimately leadership is leadership by example, not by lecture. If the Minister were prepared to rise in the House, instead of talking from his seat, he would demonstrate that he is prepared to bring in reforms and to bring controls to Crown corporations which would begin to open up Government.
The Government could begin with sunset legislation to allow Parliament to review programs which have been put in place.
It could begin the process of deregulation, for example, in the communications field where the Government still believes it is its job to decide what Canadians will be able to see and to hear, rather than give Canadians the right to decide for themselves. If the Minister would demonstrate that he had given up on the philosophy that mother Government knows better than individual Canadians what is in their best interests, then I would think he had the right to say that the Government was prepared to share with Parliament or to take initiatives in regulatory reform. Instead, what we get is cosmetics. The people of Canada demand better than that. If the Government is not prepared to give better than that to the people of Canada, let it call an election. Canadians recognize that there is an option, and they recognize that following that election we could begin the work of pruning back Government and restoring to individual Canadians a sense of dignity, a sense of worth and the ability to run their own lives free of the dead hand of Government.

Mr. Speaker, keeping to the Bill before us, I want first to commend and congratulate the committee on the work it has done, going through the legislation and determining, as anyone reading would conclude, that the legislation now being done away with is indeed obsolete.
I am listening to the arguments across the floor of the House. They should have been on the committee together. They could have worked. It may be an important thing for the Parliament of Canada, in as much as we may be doing something today that is more relevant than much of what we have done over the course of the last two years. We are actually getting rid of some legislation.
It might be a useful exercise if we now take on the task of simplifying much of the legislation that average individuals in the country have to deal with on a day-to-day basis. We have legislation that is written in such a way that by far the vast majority of Canadians are unable to understand it. We have made it almost impossible for Canadian families and individuals, even those of considerable intelligence, to pick a law, read it and understand what it says and how it will or at least ought to be applied.
For many years I have believed that one of the roles of Parliament surely must be to try to find ways to simplify the language used in legislation, not only as this Bill does, eliminating legislation that is redundant or obsolete, making it possible for people to understand not only the Income Tax Act, which is the most obvious, but other Acts that apply to individuals and families. We should devote some time and put some committees to work looking at the words used in legislation that we pass to see if there is an easier or more simple word, a word with more relevance to the day-to-day language of people in order that they cannot only see that we have done
June 28, 1983

something, but perhaps understand what it is that we have done.
I suggest to the Government that as part of the ongoing process, it not only look at legislation to determine whether it is still applicable and therefore necessary, but make an attempt to look at the language of legislation with an eye to finding new phrases, new ways of saying what we say so that the people who are affected by the laws that we produce will be able to read and understand them without having to pay out substantial sums for legal advice. It may be that they may need the advice in any event, but at least they might, in the process be able to understand why they are seeking the advice rather than follow the process they now go through.
As I said earlier, the committee has done a good job. There is a lot more to be done. Quite clearly there is even yet the requirement on all of us not only to cull out the hundreds of Acts that still exist of which the relevance is no longer apparent, but there is also the important work to be done here in the House of Commons on an ongoing basis of trying to ensure that new legislation brought in not only does what we intend it to do, but does it in a way that will provide for those who must use it the highest degree of confidence. I do not think we have been able to accomplish that.
I do not want to enter into a partisan argument about the relative merits of the Government. I think the Government by now understands that I do not agree with much of what it does. However, whether it be a Liberal or a Conservative Government, or at some point in time and NDP Government-that may be hard to picture-we have to start looking at the way we draft the laws we draft.
From my point of view, having spent 16 years of my life working with them, I find that trying to understand them is trying to understand the impossible. We do no one a service by writing laws the way we now write them. In any event, this Bill should pass hastily. We should get on to other pieces of legislation that are of importance for the future.
